passage: Neelam, you're starting your first job on Monday, so let your Gargi Masi tell you something. I was twenty-four at the insurance office in Nagpur, sure I'd picked the wrong career. I spent a whole week rehearsing one sentence, then finally asked Mrs Fernandes from underwriting, 'Could I buy you a coffee sometime?' She said yes before I finished. At the canteen I asked about exams, transfers, whether to switch to sales. She answered every question plainly. But what I carried home was one line: 'You ask good questions, Gargi. People who ask good questions do fine here.' I'd wanted a map, and I got one. I'd also wanted someone to believe in me, and I didn't know that until she did.

qa.q: Which department was Mrs Fernandes from?
qa.a: Mrs Fernandes was from underwriting.

qa.q: What did young Gargi want from that coffee besides practical answers?
qa.a: She was doubtful about her career and wanted someone experienced to believe in her, which she only realised when Mrs Fernandes said she asked good questions.

qa.q: What might Neelam take from this story for her first job?
qa.a: To gather courage and ask a senior colleague for a short chat with real questions ready, because both advice and encouragement can come from it.

qa.q: What might Mrs Fernandes have seen in that nervous junior at the canteen?
qa.a: She probably saw someone unsure but thoughtful, and chose to answer plainly and name that strength, knowing how much it helps early on.

grounding: An aunt recalls being a junior employee who asked a senior colleague for coffee, wanting practical answers and someone to believe in her.

passage: The monsoon had knocked out the power at the Kochi office, and Jomon had a train to catch in twenty minutes. Seema had waited three weeks to ask him. She caught him at the stairwell, holding two paper cups from the tea stall downstairs. "Sir, just ten minutes? I don't know if I should stay in quality testing or move to design." Jomon checked his watch, took a cup, and sat on the step. In the grey light he asked what she liked doing on her best days, then gave her two names in the design team to talk to. Seema scribbled them on her palm. As he stood, he added, "You're sharper than you think. I've seen your bug reports." She stayed on the step long after his footsteps faded, smiling at the ink on her hand.

qa.q: What was Seema holding when she caught Jomon at the stairwell?
qa.a: She was holding two paper cups from the tea stall downstairs.

qa.q: Why did Seema stay on the step smiling after Jomon left?
qa.a: Seema felt happy and encouraged because, beyond the names she wanted, an experienced colleague had told her she was sharper than she thinks 😊.

qa.q: How did Seema make the most of such a short, awkward moment?
qa.a: She asked one clear question, wrote the names down on the spot and let Jomon guide the talk, so ten rushed minutes still gave her real next steps.

qa.q: What might the conversation have been like for Jomon, with a train to catch?
qa.a: He was pressed for time but chose to sit down anyway, which suggests he wanted to help a promising junior even in a rush.

grounding: A junior woman, unsure of her path, grabs a rushed chat with a senior colleague during a storm and gets both practical steps and belief in her.

passage:
"Jomon, sorry, do you have fifteen minutes this week? For coffee?"
"Pallavi, right? From the analytics team?" He smiled. "Tomorrow, four o'clock, the canteen."
Next day Pallavi arrived early with a list on her phone.
"I've been here eight months and I don't know if I'm on a path or just doing tasks," she said. "Should I learn more coding? Move to product? Stay?"
"Good questions. What do you enjoy most on a normal Tuesday?"
"Cleaning messy data, honestly. Is that weird?"
"It's rare. And valuable." He tapped the table. "You'll be fine here, you know. People notice your work."
Pallavi's shoulders dropped. She realised that was the answer she'd most wanted, more than any course name.

qa.q: How long had Pallavi been at the company?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's shoulders dropping suggest?
qa.a: She felt relieved and reassured, because hearing that someone experienced believed in her mattered more than the practical advice.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do next to make the most of this first coffee?
qa.a: Ask Jomon if they can meet again and pick one practical step, like a project with more messy data.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Pallavi's list and questions?
qa.a: He likely sees an anxious but serious junior and feels glad to be asked, noticing her work is valuable.

grounding: Shows a junior employee asking a senior for coffee and wanting both practical answers and to hear he believes she can succeed.

passage:
I remember the message I sent Sangeeta. Four drafts. "Would you have time for a coffee sometime? I'd value your advice." She was the only senior woman in our design studio, and I, a small-town girl, had been there a year feeling like I was guessing.
We met in the café downstairs. I asked practical things: whether to specialise, how to get onto bigger clients, what to put in my portfolio. She answered each one. But the moment I still think about came at the end. She said, "You ask good questions, Vasudha. You're going to be good at this."
I went back upstairs and sat at my desk for a while before opening my laptop. Somebody experienced had looked at me and seen a future.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha and Sangeeta meet?
qa.a: In the café downstairs.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling before she asked for coffee?
qa.a: She felt unsure and anxious, writing four drafts because she had spent a year feeling like she was guessing.

qa.q: What small step could Vasudha take after this meeting?
qa.a: Follow up on one practical answer, such as updating her portfolio, and ask Sangeeta for a second meeting.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta experience when a junior asks her for advice?
qa.a: She may feel respected and a little responsible, remembering what it is like to be new.

grounding: Shows a junior asking a senior colleague for coffee and needing both practical answers and a sign that she can succeed.

passage:
Mentoring programme note, first meeting
Amandeep, eleven months in accounts, asked me for coffee after the town hall. She had a notebook with three questions underlined: stay in audit or move to tax, whether a certification is worth the time, and how to speak up with clients. We went through each. She took careful notes but her pen stopped when I said, "You're clearly capable. The question is where you'll enjoy it." She looked up and asked, "You think so?" as if nobody had said it before. She seemed to need that as much as the answers. Next step: she will shadow a tax client call next Thursday, and we will meet again the week after.
Madhav, senior manager

qa.q: How many questions had Amandeep underlined?
qa.a: Three questions.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's pen stopping suggest she felt?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and moved, as if hearing someone believe she was capable meant a great deal to her.

qa.q: What practical next step did Madhav set up, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Shadowing a tax client call next Thursday, so Amandeep can test one option with real experience.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel walking out of this first meeting?
qa.a: She may feel encouraged and less alone, with both answers and a sense that a senior believes in her.

grounding: Shows a senior's note on a junior who asks for coffee wanting practical guidance and reassurance that she can succeed.

passage:
Monday, 9 p.m.
Did something brave today, or maybe silly. I asked Tarun from the analytics team whether he'd have coffee with me this week. He has been here eight years, and everyone goes to him when a project is stuck. I've been here seven months and still don't know whether to stay in reporting or push to move to product. I typed the message four times: "Hi Tarun, I'm Madhuri from reporting. Would you have 20 minutes this week? I'd love your advice on career paths." He replied in ten minutes: "Sure! Thursday 4 pm, the café downstairs?" I actually did a little dance by the printer. What I really want to ask isn't only which team. It's whether he thinks I'm good enough to go further. I don't know if I'll dare to say that part.

qa.q: When and where will Madhuri meet Tarun?
qa.a: Thursday at 4 pm, at the café downstairs.

qa.q: What does Madhuri most want from the coffee with Tarun?
qa.a: Madhuri feels unsure and hopeful, wanting practical advice about teams but even more a sign that someone experienced believes in Madhuri.

qa.q: What could help Madhuri get the most from Thursday's coffee?
qa.a: Writing down a few specific questions, and daring to ask honestly what strengths Tarun sees.

qa.q: How might Tarun see the invitation?
qa.a: Tarun seems happy to help, replying quickly and warmly, perhaps pleased to be asked.

grounding: Shows a junior employee unsure of the path ahead asking a senior colleague for coffee, wanting both practical answers and belief.
